speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO TABLING OF EVIDENCE AND LETTER FROM MR. DREW
speechtext:
I should like to make a statement to the house regarding certain questions which have been raised with respect to the Hong Kong inquiry.
On January 29 the leader of the opposition asked if I would now table a letter from Mr. George A. Drew which the government had been asked to table on July 14, 1942.
Subsequently, on February 9, the leader of the opposition gave notice of a motion which appears on the order paper "for a copy of the evidence taken before the Duff commission in connection with dispatching Canadian armed forces to Hong Kong".
I informed the house that to comply with either of these requests it would be necessary, among other considerations, to ascertain whether the government of the United Kingdom was now prepared to withdraw its objection to the publication of certain communications, which had been made available to the commission on the express undertaking that they would not be made public.
On Friday last, February 20, I informed the house that a reply had been received on the previous day from the United Kingdom government. The reply is to the effect that if the Canadian government wish to publish the telegrams relating specifically to the dispatch of the two Canadian battalions to Hong Kong, the United Kingdom government would raise no objection, provided the telegrams were paraphrased to avoid compromising the secret cipher. However, as regards the telegrams which related to the international situation in the far east, the United Kingdom authorities regret that they cannot agree to the publication of any of those on the ground that they belong to a class of communication framed on the basis that they would not be published. The United Kingdom authorities express the opinion that the whole system of full and frank communication between governments of the commonwealth would be prejudiced if telegrams of this nature had to be prepared on the basis that they might eventually be published.
The communications relating to the international situation in the far east which the United Kingdom authorities are still unwilling to have published were at the time of the investigation considered so secret that they were seen only by the commissioner and by counsel in a conference of which it was understood that no record was to be kept. The copy of the evidence taken before the commission does not therefore include any of the communications to the publication of which the government of the United Kingdom continues to object.
These communications, however, form an integral part of the material on which the commissioner, Sir Lyman Duff, the then chief justice, based his report. This is clearly indi-
1550

Hong Kong Inquiry
cated in the report itself. I quote the following extract from page 4 of the report of the commissioner:
I had the advantage of reading a number of dispatches from the government of the United Kingdom, which I an not at liberty to reproduce, as well as 'a dispatch from the Canadian military authorities in England, which is reproduced in part, dealing with the probabilities concerning war with Japan, and my conclusion is that, having regard to the information of which the government was in possession, derived from the best sources of information open to them, nothing emerged before the departure of the expeditionary force on the 27th of October which could have been considered to be a justification for the withdrawal by Canada from the responsibility she had undertaken.
The written record does contain telegrams to the publication of which the United Kingdom takes no exception. These telegrams cannot, however, be made public in the actual form in which they appear in the evidence. To avoid' compromising the secret ciphers they must be paraphrased. In this particular, what would be produced would necessarily be an approximation to the record rather than the written record of evidence itself. It is important that this should be clearly understood.
A word now as to the letter from Mr. George A. Drew. As the house is aware, the government was asked to table this letter in 1942. On the advice of Mr. George A. Campbell, K.C., of Montreal, counsel for the government in the Hong Kong inquiry, the request was not complied with at that time. Mr. Campbell's opinion was given to the house. It will be found in Hansard for July 15, 1942, at page 4254. I quote the following extract from Mr. Campbell's opinion:
At the conclusion of the hearing for the taking of testimony in this matter, and some days before the date fixed for completion of the hearing of oral argument, all counsel concerned received notice from the commissioner requiring them on the day of the final hearing of oral argument to deliver up to the secretary of the commission any and all transcripts of evidence, exhibits and copies thereof, written arguments and copies thereof, notes of evidence and any and all other writings and documents relating in any way whatsoever to the matters in question.
It appears from Mr. Drew's communication that it purports largely to be based upon his written argument to the commissioner, of which presumably therefore he retained a copy in his possession. In his letter he gives a number of verbatim quotations from the transcript of evidence and exhibits.
Mr. Drew's letter purports to give the effect of a number of confidential communications received by the government of Canada from the government of the United Kingdom, the disclosure of which was only consented to by the government of the United Kingdom subject to a specific condition that the disclosure was to be limited to the commissioner and counsel only, and solely for the purpose of the inquiry;

and the commissioner was not permitted to reproduce these communications in his report. Any disclosure, therefore, even to the House of Commons, would in my opinion be a violation of the substance of that condition.
If, therefore, Mr. Drew's communication is tabled by you before the House of Commons I am of the opinion that you will be violating a condition under which the government of the United Kingdom consented to the disclosure to the commissioner and counsel of those telegrams.
Hon. members will see from Mr. Campbell's opinion, that, apart altogether from the ordinary rules of courtesy invariably followed in relation to communications between governments, there was a specific obligation on the part of the Canadian government to secure the consent of the United Kingdom government before a decision could be reached respecting the publication of Mr. Drew's letter.
May I remind the house of the circumstances in which Mr. Drew's letter was written. The royal commission made its report on June 4, 1942. Some weeks later, on July 11, 1942, in a lengthy letter addressed to me as Prime Minister, Mr. Drew took exception to the findings of the commissioner. In this letter, as Mr. G. A. Campbell's opinion shows, Mr. Drew discloses information which he had been informed had been imparted by the British government to the commissioner on the express understanding that it would not be made public, a condition Mr. Drew accepted by continuing to participate in the inquiry.
Mr. Drew's letter has now been examined in the light of the reply of the United Kingdom government respecting the publication of the secret communications made available by the United Kingdom government to the commission. The letter has been found to contain several references to the contents of one of the telegrams which the United Kingdom continues to be unwilling to have made public. In view of the undertaking on which this telegram was made available to the commission. the Canadian government has no choice but to decline to table the letter.
Mr. Drew may decide for himself whether he wishes to break the confidence reposed in him and to disclose information which the government of the United Kingdom wishes to have kept secret. So far as our government is concerned, we intend to have no part in any such breach of faith with the British government. Equally we do not intend to invest Mr. Drew's letter with any kind of privilege by tabling it in the House of Commons and thereby making it a public document.
As regards the tabling of the evidence, the government is of the opinion that it would have been more in accord with the feelings

Hong Kong Inquiry
of the Canadian people if the Hong Kong matter had not been revived. The report of the commission of inquiry speaks for itself. The report was made by the then Chief Justice of Canada after hearing all the evidence and all the arguments. However, as a request for a copy of the evidence has been made by the leader of the opposition, and a refusal on the part of the government to comply with that request might occasion misunderstanding and misrepresentation, the government is prepared to table the written record of the evidence. In so doing, however, it will be necessary, for reasons of security, to paraphrase the texts of cipher messages, and, for reasons which will be obvious, to make available only to the leaders on the opposition side certain confidential reports on officers and units not selected for the Hong Kong force, and certain reports or communications based on sources outside the armed forces of Canada, in cases where such reports or communications were made on the understanding that the information was to remain confidential.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO TABLING OF EVIDENCE AND LETTER FROM MR. DREW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house has listened with interest to the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) with respect to certain incidents arising out of the Hong Kong affair of some five years or more ago. I am aware that on an occasion such as this we are not allowed to debate the matter. On the other hand the practice has grown up of the government at the opening of the house making statements of this kind, at which times Your Honour has permitted brief observations by hon. members on this side of the house who may feel they have some comment that should be made.
I wish to say only three things, and to say them briefly. One of the basic rights of democracy is that parliament must know, if it wishes, what is going on or what has gone on behind the scenes. We gave up that right during the war, when the nation was in danger. Now that the war is over we think we are entitled to know the factg. The Prime Minister has indicated that certain facts will be made available. To that extent I am sure the house will be pleased.
My second observation is this: In connection with this whole Hong Kong affair I do not suppose there was any other instance in world war II where untrained and unarmed troops were sent into battle. As to who wag responsible for that, the Canadian people are entitled to know.
The Prime Minister has referred to codes uged in communications used between two countries. I am sure there is no one in the 5849-99J
house who would wish or ask that information such as that should be divulged. I think that what the house wants, and what the Canadian people want, could be given without divulging any such secrets between two nations. But if there has been incompetence somewhere in an affair of this importance, the Canadian people will want to see it exposed.
I have just one other thing to say. As I gather from the Prime Minister's remarks, he is denying us the right to have the Drew correspondence tabled. He is undertaking to table certain other information-perhaps the greater part of the evidence of the Duff commission-but certain other parts he hag indicated, ag I gathered from his remarks, that he does not feel the government can take the responsibility for tabling.
I shall conclude by saying that the government must accept full responsibility for any portion of that evidence it denies to parliament. I am sure the Prime Minister is prepared to take that responsibility. But he must take it, not the House of Commons. When the evidence comes down we will see how much has been given and how much has been held back. We cannot be left in the position of allowing another administration to excuse this administration from tabling all the information we are entitled to have.
All we on this side of the house want is the facts, and the truth, without exposing any secret codes which may exist between another country and Canada. I trust that when the evidence comes down we will find that the government has not held back anything that would help to clarify this painful episode in Canada's history.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO TABLING OF EVIDENCE AND LETTER FROM MR. DREW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say just a word? I have a distinct recollection of what happened on July 14 after the leaders of the parties on this side of the house had received a copy of the letter which Colonel Drew sent to ithe Prime Minister. On that occasion I stated that I would accept the responsibility of asking that it be tabled. Next day the Prime Minister brought down the opinion of Mr. Campbell. As I recollect, having heard the opinion of counsel no one on this side of the house pressed at that time for the tabling of the evidence.
The war is over. The resolution which occasioned this discussion calls for a copy of the evidence taken before the Duff commission in connection with dispatching Canadian, armed forces to Hong Kong. The Drew letter does not figure in that particular resolution. The Prime Minister has only to bring down the evidence with certain telegrams paraphrased and with other telegrams with-
Hong Kong Inquiry

held at the request of the British government. If that is done I believe that we shall then be able to make an appraisal of the evidence :and come to a better conclusion with respect to the Hong Kong affair.
I have always been uneasy about the Hong Kong affair, particularly because I saw some -of the men who were to go there, one of whom appeared later before the commission nnd gave me information which I believe will be found in the evidence. I am glad that the evidence is to be produced. Following the discussion which the Prime Minister had yesterday with the leaders of the groups in the house I agree that in view of the secrecy of the code used between Great Britain and Canada the telegrams cannot be disclosed in their original phraseology. However, I hope that in making the paraphrase the responsible officials will exercise particular care to see that there is accuracy in every particular. I believe that that will be done. Since this meets the object of the resolution, I hope that we shall have an opportunity of reviewing the evidence.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO TABLING OF EVIDENCE AND LETTER FROM MR. DREW
speechtext: Why should the dispatches be paraphrased rather than simply decoded?

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLANTON (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO TABLING OF EVIDENCE AND LETTER FROM MR. DREW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might be permitted to answer that question. It is within the knowledge of all hon. members that highly confidential information passes between representatives of governments which it would be of great advantage, in war or in peace, for other countries to obtain. For that reason all nations have ciphers and codes which they endeavour to keep safe. It is also well known to hon. members, through the press and otherwise, that sometimes certain nations endeavour to intercept messages in order to try to break a cipher and learn- exactly what is contained in it. And it is within the knowledge of hon. members that no small part of the allied successes during this war was due to the fact that so far as is now known- allied ciphers remained impregnable whereas enemy ciphers did not. One reason for that is that it may be possible to intercept the exact text of messages as they were sent in cipher, but in order to break them down it is almost essential to have the exact text of the message as decoded. A country having possession of those two factors certainly stood a much better chance of breaking a cipher than without them. On

Hong Kong Inquiry
that ground whenever ciphers are used they are required to be paraphrased. That is the ordinary and customary practice within government departments and between governments and it is in accordance with consistent requests from the British to ourselves and from us to them. They have made that request of us on this occasion.
I can assure hon. members that expert officers in the Departments of External Affairs and Defence are quite accustomed to paraphrasing and the results will be completely fair and accurate.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO TABLING OF EVIDENCE AND LETTER FROM MR. DREW
speechtext: Does paraphrasing mean that we shall have the government's interpretation of what the actual correspondence is?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO TABLING OF EVIDENCE AND LETTER FROM MR. DREW
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should think the hon. member had been long enough in this house to know that that would not be the desire of this government at least. There is no case where that has been shown ever to have taken place. The paraphrasing will be done by expert officials of the Department of External Affairs or of National Defence, and it will be done under very close scrutiny.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO TABLING OF EVIDENCE AND LETTER FROM MR. DREW
speechtext: After the way the Prime Minister undertook to paraphrase George Drew's position in connection with this matter, you do not need to wonder that I asked the question.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition) :
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: SIMPLIFIED FORMS FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the many representations coming to members of parliament from farmers, I would ask the Minister of Finance whether he has given consideration to simplifying Form T-l Prairie Farmers 1947 now required for taxation purposes. The title of this form would indicate that it applies to prairie farmers only. Is a similar form required from farmers in other parts of Canada?
Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT ^Minister of Finance): That is a matter that comes under the Minister of National Revenue. I will ask him to reply.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCANN (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: SIMPLIFIED FORMS FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
I have received the question of the hon. leader of the opposition through the Minister of Finance. It will be generally appreciated bjr the members of the house that there are great difficulties in securing income tax returns from farmers and difficulties in assessing those returns. It is unnecessary for me here to enumerate what those difficulties are, but with a view to clearing up some of them and giving assistance to the farmers of Canada in making their returns, officials of the Department of National Revenue have given very close study to the matter, as a result of which we got out last fall two guides. One guide is called the Prairie Farmers Income Tax Guide and Farm Account Book. That form is distributed to the farmers in Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan. Another form has been gotten out for farmers in eastern Canada. It is called the Farmers Income Tax Guide and Farm Account Book. As a result of those two guides which have been sent out, two forms have been devised on which the farmers might make their returns. One is T-l Prairie Farmers 1947, and the other is T-l Farmers, 1947.
The question has been asked, have we given consideration to simplifying these forms? The department will always give consideration to simplifying the forms and assisting the farmer in making out his return. That is the policy which is followed by the department, with

Inquiries of the Ministry
reference not only to farmers but to other people engaged in business. It is a policy followed by other countries.
Hon. members may have noticed that in the Ottawa Citizen and Ottawa Journal of last Saturday an advertisement appeared to the effect that an officer of the internal revenue department of the United States would be in Ottawa to assist United States residents in filling out their income tax returns, and in this morning's Montreal Gazette there appeared a notice to the effect that an officer of the internal revenue department of the United States would be present in Montreal to assist citizens of the United States in making out their income tax returns.
As I have said, with a view to helping the Canadian farmer make his return, these guides and these forms have been devised and sent out, and I can state that the form and guide for the prairie farmers have been very favourably received in the press, at least, and we have had a great number of applications for the form over and above the number already distributed. I think that this answers the question of the hon. leader of the opposition.
I might add that all our officers have been instructed to use the utmost courtesy and fairness in approaching the farmers and in giving the assistance which the division offers.

speechtext: If the minister will permit a supplementary question, would he look at page 5 of the form which I see he has before him, the prairie farmers' form, which requires the farmer to set out his net worth? The method of setting it out is quite complicated. My question is this. Is any other class of taxpayer asked to do a similar job to that now asked of the prairie farmer? I know of none, and if I am correct I want to know why he has been singled out to expose the last cash dollar he has in the bank, in the strong box or in his wife's stocking, or wherever people put their money. I know of no other class of citizen which have been singled out as has the western farmer to give that information. If I am wrong I shall be glad to be told so. Certainly it is not something that I sign after my accountant makes out my return.

subtopic: SIMPLIFIED FORMS FOR FARMERS

In order to arrive at a position where there may be a proper return and assessment made, if they are assessable, we have to find out their net worth position, and on that net worth position, over a period of years, to find out if possible what their income has been; and in regard to those who make the return yearly, what their average net income has been over the period of years. I do not know that there is any other way of arriving at it except to ask what assets and liabilities they have, and from that information determine their position.

subtopic: SIMPLIFIED FORMS FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
I think the answer to that must be obvious. The type of farming that is carried on in the western provinces is different from what it might be say in the Niagara peninsula. In making up a form for farmers one has to attempt to make a composite return. You could not have one return for a farmer who is in the poultry business, another for a man who is in the grain business, another for a man who is in the fruit and vegetable business or the truck gardening business, and so on. Therefore it has been decided that at least we should have two different types, one

which would cover the prairie farmers and the other which would cover the rest of the farmers of Canada.

speechtext: I beg your pardon; yes, we do. Let us clear that up right away. I hold in my hand the T-l Farmers 1947. They are exactly the same in that regard. On page 5 the farmer is asked for a net worth statement. Then I have the Prairie Farmers T-l 1947. On page 5 he is asked for a net worth statement. I wish to answer a question asked by the member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) on Thursday last, as follows:
Has the minister received communications from western Canadian beef producers and feeders that prices for finished beef are falling, apparently owing to the meat packing companies' lack of interest in bidding for finished beef? Secondly, will -the minister tell the house what measures he proposes to take to protect beef feeders from losses on their 1947-48 operations, and thus to safeguard beef supplies for Canadian consumers for the year 1949.

The answer, Mr. Speaker, is this. Representations have been received from some western producers to the effect that there is not an active demand and that prices are considered unsatisfactory. The facts are that during this year to date there has been a substantial increase in the number of cattle marketed, and prices for good quality cattle have averaged approximately $2 a hundred higher than during the same period a year ago.
The inspected slaughtering of cattle in January was 23-9 per cent greater than during January 1947. Slaughterings during the past two weeks were 39 per cent greater than the same two weeks a year ago, and to date slaughterings were 28-2 per cent higher. This would seem to disprove any argument that cattle were not moving freely. Not only was there a substantial increase in the number of cattle marketed, but the average dressed weight of beef slaughtered in January 1948 was 508 pounds per head, which was 28 pounds higher than the average dressed weight in January 1947, and 18 pounds heavier than the average dressed weight of beef slaughtered in January 1946.
During the early part of 1947 cattle slaughterings were barely sufficient to meet domestic requirements, and no surplus beef was being offered for export. Beef and cattle prices during this period were established on the basis of domestic value and not on export value. Marketings for 1948 to date have been substantially in excess of domestic requirements, and some 13,000,000 pounds of beef have been offered for export. I might add in passing that that is twice as much as we got last year, to November 1. The price provided in the 1948 beef agreement of $27.50 for choice quality beef and $26.50 for good quality beef is $3.25 higher than the price paid under the. 1927 agreement. Notwithstanding the fact that cattle marketings are in excess of domestic requirements, prices for good quality cattle are still well above their value for export based on the United Kingdom agreement.
With regard to the general level of cattle prices during 1947, good steers averaged $14.19 at Toronto. This was the highest annual average price ever recorded ,and was six cents higher than the average price of $14.13 in 1919 and more than double the average price of $6.77 in 1939. While there has been some moderate recession in cattle prices during the last two or three weeks, more particularly for

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not rise at this time to make any extended remarks. We opposed the measure on second reading, and we have opposed it consistently ever since. I rise now to move an amendment to third reading of the bill, an amendment which seeks to remove from the bill a feature which it was not the primary intention of the bill to achieve, namely that of protectionism. I move:
That the said bill be not now read the third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole for the purpose of amending it by inserting after the word "Canada" in the second line of section 3, subsection (1) the following words:
"from any one of the following countries, namely Cuba, Dominican Republic, Guatemala, Haiti, Panama. El Salvador, Switzerland, Union of 'Soviet Socialist Republics, United States of America and its possessions, Venezuela."
Section 3 (1) would then read in this way:
No person shall import or attempt to import into Canada from any one of the following countries, namely Cuba, Dominican Republic, Guatemala, Haiti, Panama, El Salvador, Switzerland, Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, United States of America and its possessions, Venezuela, any goods listed or of the classes described an schedules I, II or III except in accordance with a permit issued by the minister and, subject to this act and the regulations, the minister may issue, vary, or revoke permits for the import of such goods.
I shall take only a moment to comment on this amendment. The countries, the names of which I have read, are those which have been designated as scheduled countries in P.C. 4678 passed by the government under the foreign exchange control act, and under which these restrictions are now being carried out.

Foreign Exchange Conservation
This is the order in council, with some amendments, under which the government has been acting for more than three months.
The problem the government is seeking to solve by this bill is to conserve United States dollars. In order to conserve United States dollars the government has already divided the countries with which we do business into two groups: (1) dollar countries or, in point of fact, countries that have no dollar problem; and (2) countries which are, like ourselves, having difficulty in finding United States dollars to pay for purchases made in that country. The amendment I have moved means that we limit the bill to the policy of dollar conservation and exclude from it the features of wider protection. The bill without the amendment means that it is not an exchange conservation measure solely, but rather a bill providing additional protection against imports from all countries.
As it is at present the bill, whatever else it does, is a measure of ironclad protection. It means that this self-styled low-tariff government is making its present difficulty the occasion to introduce a wholly unnecessary and vicious type of tariff restrictions practically unknown in any democratic country.
We are not in this amendment, opposing the dollar conservation features of the measure; but the amendment would cut out the additional features of protection which are not necessary for the purpose I have mentioned.

At that time I said on behalf of this party that we would vigorously oppose it, and that we would oppose it in the house and in the constituencies and do our best-

speechtext:
In these two months, Mr. Speaker, the evils of this bill have become much more apparent than they were then. The evils to which I wish to refer briefly are, first, the evil of personal power, and, second, the fact that this bill is not really an emergency bill at all, which has become clearer and clearer as we have gone on.
First a word about personal power. We on this side have been complaining a good deal in the last two years about orders in council; but once this bill becomes law we shall look back on orders in council almost as the halcyon days of freedom, because this bill gives power to one minister so broad it is really hardly an exaggeration, indeed it is no exaggeration to say that he himself can tear up orders in council and make the effect of them nugatory.
Everything depends on this minister; and I wish to point out further, rather regretfully, that there has not been-I must admit this- as much protest from the country as we would have expected. Then there is a quotation, I presume from the Bank of Canada's report:

Then the writer concludes:
If Mr. Howe wants industry to take his dollar saving program seriously he will have to take it seriously himself.
So much for the time. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has not helped us very much on that. To use his own phraseology, he has become a bit tied to the use of the word "months", and that seems to have affected his comments since that time.
Coining to the more important part, what is really being done to end the emergency, we have nothing at the moment except vague and, I must add, unconvincing statements from the minister os to what great things are being done or what great things are to be done to increase exports to the United States. He has never been very convincing on that and, as I have said, it is left entirely in the air. Meantime, however, as the house will remember, by the financial policy of the government, and particularly by what was done in June, 1946, we have taken one step which operates vitally to put off the day when the emergency ends. That is to say, we have successfully cut off United States investment in this country.
I want to say a word to recall to the minds of hon. members the position we were in in June, 1946. We seemed at that time to have achieved a kind of rough and ready balance. We seemed-and in retrospect it looks even clearer-to have reached the point where the finance department was allowing a good deal of freedom, and where more and more freedom could have been achieved and our situation worked out. But whatever the reason was, whether it is because the finance department somehow cannot believe that

things can work through freedom, whether they believe that controls are the only means of doing things, at any rate in June, 1946, they took the action that we know, and from that time on, our supply of United States dollars and gold fell. I believe the figure in June, 1946, was SI,624 million, and it fell last November to something in the neighbourhood of S500 million.
Worse than that, we have created a situation in the United States where, as I said in this house a few days ago, our dollars and securities are wandering around like orphans. "Orphan", I believe, is the word they use. Our dollar sells below ninety cents and our securities at an even greater discount, and in my opinion we are creating a situation where Americans, who have regarded us as the very best investment market, are thoroughly irritated at what we have done. And we go from bad to worse.
The action that was taken then reminds me of an old epitaph with which we are all familiar. I discovered today that it was found somewhere on the tombstone of an Italian valetudinarian: "I was well; I would be better; I am here." I hope that nothing like that is our fate, but I suggest that those who disturbed the balance in June, 1916, took on a considerable responsibility.
Now a word to recall the circumstances attending the introduction of the bill, which circumstances do not commend it. First of all, there was the withholding of information- I believe that is the proper word-and the rapidly worsening figures all through last summer, and then there was the sudden action in the middle of November. We had been trying to get information here in this house even before parliament adjourned in July and we got none. Second, there was neglect to summon parliament, which could have been summoned, because, after all, this matter was under review, as the Minister of Finance has told us, from away back, months before; I believe he said it was in August or July. Finally, there was the disregard of an undertaking or a statement of intention, or what you will, which the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley) gave in connection with the foreign exchange control board.
I will not split hairs about that and ask whether it was a solemn undertaking or a promise. I do not know what the difference is between a solemn promise and any other promise. I consider every promise a solemn promise. I want that to be clear. I used the words "statement of intention". That is perhaps more correct than the word "promise". However, I should have thought that a statement of intention, particularly perhaps from a minister with the moral authority in this

Foreign Exchange Conservation
house which the present Minister of Justice has always had, was as good as putting it on your bond and affixing all the red seals around it, something as good as anyone could want. I will say no more on that. It was treated as such anyway, as the hon. member for Stan-stead reminds me.
There was little public protest; and it is a sad reflection, in my opinion, on the level of political consciousness in this country that there has not been more protest. I sometimes think people hardly realize what is going on under their very eyes, and that being so, it is all the more necessary that we who are members of parliament, who presumably think about these things and take them seriously, should have concern for a matter of this kind and not treat it lightly.
1 suppose it is true to say that in the long history of British institutions, of institutions that we rely upon, institutions that have brought us where we are, there have been many times when action such a!s has been taken by this government, first of all in withholding information; second, in dealing in so arbitrary a manner with a situation such as this, without calling parliament, and, third, in going back on a statement made by a responsible minister-it is, I say, no exaggeration to suggest that lesser things than these have brought governments toppling down more than once in our history.
My final point is this. I suppose one can say that freedom is the second greatest thing in the world. Faith is the greatest, and1 the church is the special guardian of faith. But surely this House of Commons should be the special guardian of freedom, and. therefore I suggest earnestly that everyone in this house who believes in freedom should vote against this bill, for in this bill freedom is the issue.

The principle involved in both those amendments highlights one of the reasons for our objecting to this bill, namely the government's insistence on applying the mon-diseriminatory principle at the present time.
We argued at the outset, and in our view the minister has not answered our arguments, that in effect this is discrimination against the United Kingdom and other soft currency
countries, and further that it has no real bearing on the main purpose of the bill which is to save United States dollars.
When the debate on the second1 reading was in progress another of the objections to the bill, which we put forward, was that it involved a ban on fresh fruits and vegetables which we regarded as inimical to the health of the Canadian people. Our friends of the Progressive Conservative party applauded us at that time and indeed echoed our sentiments.
When we were in committee of the whole at least one member of the Progressive Conservative party, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman), who just now applauded my remarks, spoke in support of our opposition to item 87 in schedule I. I regret to say, however, that when the time came for a vote in committee on that item our friends of the Progressive Conservative party voted with the government to retain it.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) has just had something to say about the feeling of the people in the country as to this bill. If I heard him correctly he said he was amazed there was not more protest against the bill in general. I would say to him there is one feature about which there has been considerable protest, on the part of housewives in particular, and it is this ban on fresh fruits and vegetables; and I call as one of my principal witnesses the hon. member for Rosedale. I am indeed sorry that our Progressive Conservative friends did not see fit to join us in our vote against that item when we were in committee. I remind the house that the vote was 43 to 23; but had the Progressive Conservatives who were present at that time voted with us, the clause would have been defeated.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this raises some question about the consistency of the opposition of the Progressive Conservative party to this measure, to which the leader of the opposition referred. The fact is that when the members of the official opposition were faced with this vegetable item, which to them was a question of protection or non-protection, they voted for protection. That is another of the reasons we gave earlier for our opposition to this bill, namely, that it is a highly protectionist measure and that it has and will have all the damaging effects to our economy of any of the restrictive trade measures we have had in the past. The demonstration we had, particularly in committee, of Liberal members rising and telling the house that if vegetable growers in their part of the country could be assured that this
Foreign Exchange Conservation

protection would be maintained they could produce greater quantities behind that wall of protection, indeed must go down in the pages of Hansard as a sorry story in the annals of the Liberal party. We call to witness all the arguments Liberals have used in the past about the dangers to our economy of restrictive tiade policies, and suggest that for these reasons this bill should not receive the support of this house.
Another of at least four reasons we stated earlier for objecting to this .bill was the unwillingness of the government to reimpose price ceilings in Canada on goods of a class or kind the importation of which from the United States was subject to restriction or embargo. We felt then and, having given the measure complete study clause by clause in committee, we still take that position, that the effect of this measure without price control on those items is to exploit the Canadian people at the expense of what is, after all, in its effect a protectionist policy.
So, Mr. Speaker, I submit that our consistent opposition to this measure has been well founded, and for the reasons I have stated we will oppose it on third reading.

Mr. Speaker, I am referring to the agreement which has been made by Britain with Czechoslovakia and which is driving the mother country away from the tariff protection which she had under preferences, as the cause and effect of Bill No. 3, and Britain has to seek food from Europe and other countries, including Denmark and Argentina. You will notice it is in the schedule. Britain has been practically forced out of the preference by the policy of this government. She has to provide food for
47,000.000 people and she cannot get it from Canada. She has had to go to Russia. She has made a treaty with them, a bargain. She has had to bargain with Poland. She has made one with Czechoslovakia. Russia made lengthy trade treaties with Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, Sweden. Norway, Denmark, Iceland, France, Great Britain, Uruguay and other countries.
Where has our trade gone? We had trade with all those countries and so had the mother country'; so had New Zealand and so had Australia. They have been kicked out. We know what happened in Manchester and Birmingham under British preference. They did a tremendous amount of business with India, but now that business goes to the United States and Russia. Russia has also made an agreement with Italy, with Sweden, with Belgium and with some of our other allies to the injury of trade with Britain and the dominions. I will not refer to any more now, but they have made them with Hungary, Roumania. Britain did a large trade with Roumania in food and many other things like that. A great writer on all these soviet trade treaties, Peter Dene, said ably in his conclusions on the soviet raid on trade:
This picture of post-war trade agreements concluded by Russia and her satellites shows how great are the distortion and shrinkage of trade and economic activity in a vital part of Europe. Before the war all these countries did

a far larger trade with Germany, with Britain and other western lands, and in many cases with one another. The great bulk of all this has vanished. What remains comprises only the most essential-but also the most paltry- exchanges.
We cannot now, under preferential trade, do any particular trade with the empire. The A.R. Clarke and Company Limited, a fine patent and finished leather manufacturing concern was, before the war, located in my constituency. They did trade with Asia Minor and almost every other country in Europe and the far east under preference, and with India, but they have had to close up. Now the United States or some other country will get that trade. This writer, Peter Dene continues:
Very striking, 'among other things, is the inability of the much-vaunted soviet system to supply its satellites or anyone else with manufactured goods; raw materials are still the staples of Russia's exports. The fact, and its lessons, should be noted. As for the soviet satellites, a story current in Poland summarizes neatly what the present situation means for them. "What are the trade relations between Poland and Russia?" asked a foreigner.
"Oh! most cordial!" answers a Pole. "We are sending them our textiles, and in return they are taking our coal."
Did you ever hear of such a system as that? Britain did a large trade with Poland for many years. I am not going to vote for this particular bill without a protegt. I believe this particular bill will be the greatest economic gamble this country has ever made. If we abandon the mother country so far as preference is concerned, we shall never get preferences back. The government have not a mandate from the people. They have refused to give the people the facts, and they have not been altogether fair in giving the House of Commons the facts. As Mr. Wilgress said the other day, they cannot change this agreement one iota, and, as I say. we are only conducting a post mortem. It has been signed, sealed and delivered by twenty-one countries and it is retroactive to November 17. Mr. Wilgress sent a wire on behalf of the Canadian delegation from Havana saying that 800 amendments had been moved by twenty-one nations, Canada proposed none and not one was accepted there. Is that, the kind of business we want to transact in this country? I say no.
The plan is all wrong. We shall find that there will be widespread unemployment and the reimposition of controls which will hamstring business and retard the development of our national resources, for want of a national policy for our resources. What have we done to save United States dollars since 1923, when I raised this matter? Have we a national coal
and fuel policy today? No. Have we an oil supply, a policy of pipelines and real development? No. Have we developed the water powers of this country? No. We are even exporting power to United States industries along the St. Lawrence from power companies in Ontario and Quebec.
The present government has strangled the St. Lawrence waterway. They are to vote in Washington on Friday on the St. Lawrence waterway. I introduced resolutions concerning this waterway practically every year from 1923 onward. What is the policy of this government? Apparently the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) last fall appointed another useless commission to investigate the Lachine part of it. It will be going on in this way until doomsday if the present government has anything to do with it.
We should) develop our own natural resources. Last year we had a chance to save the base metals of Labrador for the people of Newfoundland and for the benefit of this country. As the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) suggested last night, smelters should1 be erected to process this Labrador ore. We had a long discussion about these Labrador natural resources being handed over to a private company in the bill I opposed here last year. That is one of the most fatal mistakes we have ever made. This great hand-out is being made to private interests for their own power and gain. These various American interests are largely run from New York by United States citizens, and they have the best sites all over Canada, of our raw materials and natural resources.
I am a great admirer of the United1 States, but I think they would1 appreciate us more if we told them our side of the story. They do not want to take unfair advantage of us. We know what they did in the last two wars and we know what they are planning to do under the Marshall plan. They are a great people and they would respect us more if we told the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth about this particular bill, and our side of the story after the last war. We have been told nothing about this bill; we have been blindfolded and kept in the dark.
I am sorry to see the Minister of Reconstruction and1 Supply doing this work. This country stands at the darkest hour in its economic history. I do not know where the empire is going or whether the empire will survive. England is facing her darkest days. The Marshall plan is part and parcel of this bill because they will expect United States dollars for the food Canada supplied1 for Europe under this bill. It would be far better for the United States to hand over all that

We hope Britain will weather this storm. She can if she is left to herself. Britain is a great nation. She stood by us in two wars.
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), who has done splendid work and whose speeches I always like to hear, has complained about British Columbia not having a cabinet minister. In the last parliament which was dissolved in 1945, we had as many representatives from the Toronto district as there were members of our party from five or six of the nine provinces; yet the Toronto district has never had a cabinet representative since 1935-Toronto, the greatest city in the dominion, the centre of education, the leader in municipal institutions in the country, Canada's greatest manufacturing, taxpaying city and the centre of a great area of agricultural development. Mr. GLEASON BELZILE (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 114, to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, 1944.
He said1: Yesterday when the resolution preceding this bill was introduced in the house the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) asked a few questions respecting this measure. It was therefore deemed advisable that a short statement of the purpose and working of the act of 1944 and of the objects of this bill be given the house.
As hon. members are well aware, the primary purpose of the act was to fill a- gap in the credit system which has been developed in Canada to meet the needs of agriculture. That gap related chiefly to the provision of intermediate credit and certain types of short term credit to farmers for the improvement and development of farms, and for the improvement of living conditions thereon. The act aims at assisting the average farmer, who in the past frequently has not been able to secure bank credit for these purposes. It aims, moreover, at providing credit in a form and under terms and conditions which are convenient and suited to the needs and conditions of the particular farm borrower.

This bill provides for the following two amendments to the act of 1944. First, it extends the operation of the act for a further period of three years from March 1 next. Second, it broadens the field of loans in respect of which security may be taken by way of mortgage. Under the present act there are two limits on the amount of bank loans for farm improvement purposes that may be guaranteed by the Minister of Finance. First, there is a dollar limit of $250,000,000; second, there is a time limit of three years from the commencement of the existing act, which was March 1, 1945. The dollar limit allows a great deal of scope for further lending activity, but the time limit becomes effective by the end of this month. By this bill we close off the old pool of loans at what the amount will be at the end of February, and then provide for a new pool to start on March 1 next and to run for a further period of three years, provided that the amount does not exceed the balance of the dollar limit, roughly $215 million. Thus, in respect of the approximately $35,000,000 amount of loans made up to the end of this month, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will pay all losses incurred by each bank, provided that they do not exceed ten per cent of the total eligible loans made by the bank. Then, in so far as new loans are

Farm Improvement Loans
made after March 1 next and up until the end of three years therefrom or until the total amount of loans made by all banks from March 1, 1945, equals $250 million, we will pay losses of each bank up to ten per cent of the loans made by the bank.
With reference to the second amendment, the situation is now that mortgage security can be taken only where the loan exceeds $2,000 and the period for repayment is longer than five years. This has been found unduly restrictive and has tended to prevent the making of certain loans which otherwise would be made if mortgage security could be given.
The new amendment makes it possible to take mortgage security if the loan is made for the purpose of financing the construction, repair or alteration of, or making of additions to any building or structure on a farm; or if the loan is made for any other purpose, exceeds $2,000 in amount, and extends for longer than five years.
In closing my remarks, I wish to say that the banks have continued to give excellent co-operation in promoting the objectives of this legislation, both in the way of publicity and generally in making the provisions of the act known.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will agree that the passage of a bill such as we now have before us is certainly essential. As the parliamentary assistant has ably pointed out, the scope of the provisions of the bill is wide indeed.
The original act, which this bill amends, provided for loans for farm improvements for such things as the purchase of farm implements, livestock, electrical systems, fencing, farm buildings and general improvements. Anyone who has travelled much in the rural sections of Canada will know that on almost any farm there is room for vast improvements.
I believe almost any farmer could use many hundreds of dollars to provide for improvements both in his farm equipment and in the home in which he and his family live. Therefore I believe the scope of this act has given the banks an opportunity to be of real service to Canadian agriculture.
The act when first introduced to the house in 1944 promised a good many things, and the then minister of finance stated in one place what he hoped the Farm Improvement Loans Act would do by way of reducing farm implement prices. Prior to the passing of that act the farm implement companies had financed their own credit w'hen they placed machines out on credit. The excuse was made by the implement companies that the reason their implement prices had been kept high
was that they had lost a lot of money through bad debts. The then minister of finance, speaking in the house on June 6, 1944, as reported at page 3609 of Hansard, said the following with respect to the farm improv-ment loans bill:
When the scheme is in operation the great majority of farmers will be able to arrange a loan at the bank and pay cash to the manufacturer or dealer for his machinery and equipment. The lower rate of interest payable on farm improvement loans will constitute a direct saving to the farmer, and I am also hopeful that this method of financing will make a real contribution to a reduction in prices of farm implements and equipment.
I submit that the implement companies have taken advantage of the fact that there is an act such as this which provides a different means of credit for the purchasing of farm implements, and have absorbed the former costs of credits. This is well shown by the profits implement companies have made in the past few years.
The Farm Improvement Loans Act provides for interest at the rate of five per cent. I would say, in view of the general interest rates prevailing throughout Canada at the present time, that the interest rate is too high. The Canadian farm loan board is in business for the making of farm loans for the purchase of land, and that board is able to operate with a reasonable profit at an interest rate of four and one-half per cent. The Canadian farm loan board, in its report, shows assets in 1947 amounting to $22,909,000, acquired mainly through loans, and it shows that it made a profit of over $165,000. That $165,000 profit was made in respect of loans totalling $22,909,000 at a rate of interest which is one-half of one per cent less than is provided in the present measure. The Canadian farm loan board must borrow' the money it uses for reinvestment purposes, and it has borrowed that money from the federal government at a rate of three and one-half per cent. So I say that the interest rate provided in the present measure is indeed high.
A further incentive to chartered banks has been the guarantee against loss up to ten per cent of the aggregate amount of their loans. Through this measure the government is saying to the banks, "We will give you the high rate of interest of five per cent, and also guarantee you against loss up to ten per cent of the aggregate amount of your loans. We will allow you to make the profits, and the Canadian people, through the government, will pay any losses you are likely to sustain."
I say this is leaning over backwards in an attempt to make very easy and profitable business for the chartered banks of Canada.
Farm Improvement Loans

I was pleased to hear the parliamentary assistant read some statistics as to the amount of business accomplished through this measure thus far. If I understood him correctly he said that something more than $31,000,000 had been made in loans thus far under the act. The number of loans is approximately 40,000. That works out to an average loan of a little less than $800. On the basis of the total farms in Canada, which was 732,000 in 1941, it amounts to only $43 per farm. If the money were spread over the three years it would mean that, through this measure, the average farmer has received somewhat more than $14 a year with which to make improvements on his farm. I submit that such a small sum of money will do very little toward providing the improvements that are necessary on farms from one end of Canada to the other.
The past few years have been relatively prosperous years. In my opinion they have been years in which our banks would be likely to think these would be good loans that would be repaid. If during the last three years the total loans amounted to only $31,000,000, when, times were good, then I submit that when times are not as good as they are today, when farm prices are lower as they are certain to be, this measure will not provide for the improvements that will be absolutely necessary on farms across Canada.
I think one of the reasons why farmers have not taken advantage of this measure more than they have was the experience they had during the nineteen thirties. During those years when they were unable to meet their interest payments they found that their debts increased each succeeding year. I regret that there is no crop failure clause in this bill under which farmers would not have their debts increased in years of crop failure. The fact that there is no crop failure clause together with the high interest rates no doubt accounts to a considerable extent for the fact that this act has not been used more.
In looking over the statistics provided by the bureau of statistics in connection with chartered banks for the period 1943 to 1946, I find that their investments in securities have increased much more than their loans. During that period, for each dollar of increase by way of loans the chartered banks increased their investment in securities by $4.30. The fact is that, even with a guarantee against loss amounting to ten per cent and the high rate of interest, the banks found it more favourable to invest in government securities. By that policy the people of Canada are being made to bonus the banks and keep them in business.

The total loans which the chartered banks may make under this act and still be eligible for the ten per cent guarantee is $250,000,000, but actually the loans made amounted to only $31,000,000. That represents twelve per cent of what the banks could have lent under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I say that the banks have done a twelve per cent job. They have not accomplished what the then minister of finance said in 1944 it was hoped they would. The then minister of finance is reported on page 3608 of Hansard of June 6, 1944, as follows:
It is considered that a guarantee of ten per cent of the aggregate amount of loans made by one bank will be sufficient to offset the special risks attaching to farm improvement loans, yet will not be so large as to result in reckless lending without regard to the prospect of repayment. The amount of the guarantee is not, of course, the only factor that will influence the volume of loans. The attitude of the banks is important, and I have reason to believe that they will welcome the opportunity to extend their field of usefulness to farmers.
Whether they welcomed, the opportunity^ or not, they certainly have not done the job through this bill which was necessary to improve efficiency in farming and to better the home conditions under which the farmer has to live. If we are to get sufficient money into the hands of farmers with which to buy necessary new machinery, with which to build the buildings that are necessary on our farms and provide for the host of improvements that come under this particular measure we must nationalize the chartered banks of Canada. If that is done, then money could be lent to agriculture at a cost which would be much less than the five per cent provided here, perhaps one-half the figure.

I know that this legislation has been of some benefit to the farmers of this country, but I do not think it is the final answer to the question of intermediate farm credit. I have a few criticisms to offer in connection with the bill in general.
My first criticism would be that the interest rate is too high. Anyone who has studied the history of agricultural credit in the older countries which have had a great deal of experience in the lending of money for agricultural purposes will agree that five per cent is too high a rate of interest. It is established, in Britain, particularly, that money lent for agricultural purposes should not be charged an interest rate of more than three and a half per cent. The interest rate under this bill, five per cent, is, in my opinion, too high.
There is no provision in this bill, unless it is made in the regulations, which I have not seen or read, for the lending of money for clearing land. Provision is made for the lending of money for fencing, drainage, diking and things of that sort, but there is no provision for lending money for the clearing of land. I think that is a shortcoming in the bill. Many people are trying to develop forest farms, quite a number of them in the riding I have the honour to represent. I suggest that many of our farm ventures in the future will be forest farm ventures, and therefore provision should also be made in the bill for the lending of money for the purchase of a small portable mill, just as a person can now borrow under the bill to buy a tractor or other farm machinery.
The total of loans made in British Columbia to date under this bill is about SS00.000. and comparing that with the $11,000,000 odd lent in Alberta, one would say that the act is not functioning very well in British Columbia.
One other criticism. I do not see any arrangements made for the lending of money to those raising feather-bearing animals. Loans can be made to those raising fur-bearing animals, and in my opinion some provision should be made for lending money to poultry farmers and also to bee farmers.
I am going to support this legislation because I think it is of some assistance to the farmers of this country, but I think the government should consider introducing federal legislation which will assist those who support credit unions. To mobilize the credit resources of the credit unions of Canada, we should have enabling legislation to make it possible for these organizations to work under a federal scheme. The credit unions of this country have a total capital of approximately $200 million, and if we had the proper type of legislation for the development of credit unions for rural purposes we would soon have a large fund in this country provided by the farmers themselves. If we enmesh, as it were, the people who are concerned with the administration of their own affairs we shall find that way much more successful than our present way of doing business.
The farmers of this country, particularly in the west, put their savings into banks and insurance companies. The banks and insurance companies, we might say, control the savings of the farmers of this country, and at the same time the banks of this country control the lending of money to the farmers. I would like to see that condition changed. I would like to see this government-and this is not a radical suggestion, not even a socialist suggestion- pass enabling legislation that would make it possible for the farmer organizations to develop credit unions to a much greater extent on a national basis, so that farmers could invest their own savings in what might be termed their own rural banks, and thereby have some control in their administration and in the lending of money for agricultural purposes.
During the past three years we have invested in industry in this country something like over $800 million a year. During the past year we have invested in agriculture, under the Canadian Farm Loan Act something under $3,000,000, and under this act, approximately $10,000,000 a year. When we consider that the capital value of agriculture in this country is approximately $5,000 million, with an annual production of $1,500 million, and that we have an investment of $800 million a year in industry as compared with $13,000,000 a year invested in agriculture,
Farm Improvement Loans

we must realize that agricultural credit is not being supplied in sufficient quantities to develop agriculture as it should be developed at this time.
I repeat the suggestion I made the other evening. I believe the whole question of agricultural credit in this country should be referred for study to the committee on agriculture and colonization where witnesses can be called and the views obtained of representatives of farmer organizations in this country. But in the meantime, realizing that this bill contains certain benefits for the farmers and that under the present scheme of things it is necessary, I intend to support it.

government on a bill that has produced only a total of $31,000,000 in three years. Without question I think the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario is correct, that there have been larger amounts of money in the farmer's pockets, and possibly a shortage of goods has made it unnecessary for him to borrow, or made it impossible for him to borrow the amounts for capital equipment that he might otherwise have done. which many of them have at the present time with private institutions and on which the interest rate is comparatively high. I believe that would develop much faster than we can estimate at the present time.

An act to encourage the provision of intermediate term and short term credit to farmers for the improvement and development of farms . . .
In this country there should be provision for a lending institution which can use money created by the parliament of Canada for the use of the people of Canada in this kind of development. It makes it possible for the chartered banks, privately owned institutions, to make loans under a pretty good guarantee at a pretty fair rate of interest, and they are very unlikely to lose. That being the case, I see no reason why even this government, who time and again, through the voice of their Minister of Agriculture, have claimed to be the fathers of co-operative enterprise, have not included among those who have the right to make loans under the guarantee the credit unions of the country.
In Saskatchewan we have, I believe, about 182 of them, besides a central organization which has, as its membership, co-operatives and credit unions. If that suggestion were adopted I do not think it would be very long until this government, or any government sitting across the way, would recognize the value of such action and take steps to encourage further development of people-owned or co-operative banks of that kind, where the lending of the money, whether under government guarantee or not, would be supervised by people who have a definite interest in the institution making the loan, and where the decision would be made as to whether the loan was a good one.

Co-operative enterprise in the shape of these credit unions is private enterprise, infinitely more private than some of the monopolies which at the present time exercise such economic control over certain natural resources and business institutions that no individual less financially strong can possibly hope to compete with them in that field. In the field of co-operate enterprise, however, which is distinctly private and distinctly voluntary, these people can learn and do learn successfully to operate their own co-operative banks with their own money. They lay that money

out in loans under the careful supervision of a credit committee according to decisions made at their annual meetings attended by members of the institutions.
I suggest that if this government would make it possible for these institutions to receive the same treatment as that accorded the chartered banks which are now lending money under this act or any other assistance act that is passed, and if in doing so the government would also encourage the development of such institutions so that there could be built up and organized credit unions and co-operative banks in the country, it would prove to all members of this house and to the people at large that it is possible to have publicly owned banks operating successfully, efficiently and in the interests of the public who will produce the things that this country needs so badly.

It was passed for a term of three years, which term will expire next Saturday night, I suppose, and this 'bill enables it to continue for three years more. If this kind of bill is necessary, and I do not see why the house passed it if they did not 'believe it was necessary; if it is essential to have this kind of institution, then why in the name of goodness should we limit its lifetime to three years? If the government really 'believes that it is a good act, why should it not extend the act for at least ten years; or has the government some benevolent idea that at the end of the next three years it will have an improvement to offer? If so, let the government tell us what that improvement is and we will congratulate them upon it. But why limit the terms of this act to three years? If they believe that it is for the general good of agriculture and, therefore, of the country, I cannot see any object in bringing in this bill unless it is extended for at least ten years, and I would say even longer. Mr. VICTOR QUELCH (Acadia); I have just a few comments to offer on this bill. We in this group support the bill because we believe it serves a useful purpose; but, as we said when the bill was first introduced in 1944, we believe the rate of interest is too high, having in mind the fact that the government guarantees losses up to ten per cent. However, I do not feel like joining with some of the other speakers in criticizing the measure on the ground that the amount of business that has been done is small.
I would not at this time advise any farmer to go into debt, because at the present time the prices of everything the farmer has to buy are at top levels and there is no guarantee today that in the not far distant future the prices of the things he has to sell may not have gone down. If a farmer now loads himself with debt he may have to pay that debt back at greatly reduced prices. Therefore it is fortunate that this -act has not been utilized to a greater extent than it has been, and I am hoping that it will not need to be resorted to, to any great extent.
I realize, however, that there will always be a certain number of farmers who will have to make use of legislation of this kind. You remember how in the early days it used to be possible for farmers to buy machinery from the machinery companies without making a cash payment down. A farmer could buy a binder and pay for it in three years. Today the situation is different. If you want a binder or
a combine you have to pay cash, and if you have not the cash you have to go to a finance corporation and borrow the money. When you go to a finance corporation you pay very high rates; you pay finance charges and a high rate of interest. In view of the fact that some farmers have to buy machinery when they have not the cash, it may be a good thing to have legislation of this kind under which they may get loans at a lower rate.
I would not take the stand that it is not advisable to use this measure to any great extent if at this time we had a long-term program of stabilizing agricultural prices. If agricultural prices were stabilized at parity level for the future, then a farmer could go ahead with full confidence and borrow from an institution of this kind. So far we do not have that. We have no legislation to guarantee prices beyond 1949, as far as wheat is concerned. The Agricultural Prices Support Act is a transitional measure; it may be here today and gone tomorrow for all we know. We are hoping that the government this session will bring down legislation to stabilize agricultural prices in future, at a parity level. Until that is done, however, I repeat that I think farmers would be wise to avoid borrowing, as much as they possibly can. Most of us remember what happened after the last war, when so many farmers borrowed money. They paid high prices for the things they bought; they paid high interest rates, and after a few years they were repaying those loans with sixty cent wheat, though the debts were incurred at a time when wheat was $2 a bushel. I remember that, as I think all hon. members remember it. With that in mind, it will be a good thing for farmers if they can get by without having to use this legislation. We have a number of questions to ask, but we shall have to wait until the committee stage is reached.

Mr. Speaker, this bill is entitled, "An Act to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, 1944." I am convinced that this amendment is designed solely to protect the institutions which are lending the money for these farm improvements, and for that reason I may be more or less critical as we proceed to deal with the various clauses of the bill. I consider it unfortunate that we have the trend which is evident on the part of our rural population, and particularly the younger people, toward the larger urban centres, which indicates that they are losing their interest in the rural life of the community. I also think it is unfortunate that those who reside in the urban centres do not seem to appreciate how much the future economic welfare of this country depends upon the basic industry of agriculture; and I think that is the case in other countries as well. So my suggestion would be that rather than seek any restrictions such as those imposed in this bill we might encourage those who are in a position to lend money to have greater confidence in the future agricultural development of this nation so as to be ready to assume some credit risk.
There is evidence in the bill of a lack of confidence in the future productive capacity of the nation. I make the appeal that, in due time, our urban centres must come to appreciate the contributions made to the economic welfare of the dominion by our basic producers, including those engaged in agriculture, our fishermen, those who work in the mines and in the forests.
When we travel through life we think of our railroads; we think of the police force which protects us, the firemen who protect our property. But, in a sense, none of these is basic. So my appeal is simply to make it

I repeat that this measure to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act conveys only one thought to me, and that is greater security for the lender and less confidence in the future of Canada for those who must borrow.

I do not think one can assume that from these loans. Farm Improvement Loans
months. It costs a lot to service them, more than the actual interest rate, but I do not think it has any bearing at all on what one would call the normal rate of interest.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: I realize what was said and I agree with it. I know that the service costs on short-term loans are higher than they are on long-term loans. But this is what I have in mind. subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: I am inclined to think that was directed at me, and unless I am greatly mistaken it was. The value of money is fixed by its interest rates. It starts with exchanges, and where you borrow; it runs into farm loans, housing loans, bank loans and all that sort of thing. With the greatest respect, Mr. Chairman, I think what I did say was entirely relevant; and I am anxious to know, for example-because we get wonderful leadership from this government in some things- whether it was the idea of the government that during the next three years, having regard only to $250 million, if you like-I said that with my tongue in my cheek because it is more money than I can conceive of-this policy of five per cent interest represented the government's view as to the future money market in this country in that period of time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: I have no desire to go beyond the confines of the act, nor do I think any other member of the committee wishes to do so. subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the caisse populaire is not a rival of the farm loan board, but rather provides funds in smaller amounts to meet seasonal needs?
