speechtext:
No
doubt when the Farm Improvement Loans Act, 1944, was brought into force the government intended that it should serve a useful purpose. They undertook to guarantee the lending institutions, that is the chartered banks, any loss up to ten per cent of the $250 million, in case that much should be loaned. Now, after three years, we find the government extending this act; but during the period it has been in force, only about $30,000,000 in loans have been taken up. I think it is quite clear that the act has not operated to the extent the government may have hoped it would, and I feel one of the reasons, as some of my colleagues have already stated, is that the interest rate is far too high.
The senior parliamentary assistant has told the committee this evening that he does not consider as normal the period of time this act has been in operation. One is disturbed if he is to take from that remark the suggestion that we can look forward to a period which is not normal. On account of that condition we are told1 that the government does not see fit to bring down the interest rate to one at which farmers can secure loans.
I feel there must be a real reason why the farmers have not gone to the banks and secured1 loans, or why the banks have not seen fit to give those loans. I find that in 1941 the total farm debts, including mortgages and
Farm Improvement Loans

agreements of sale, amounted to $799 million. That is a formidable amount of diebt on the farm population of this country. It has already been indicated in this debate that the lack of machinery on our farms is an urgent problem. Then, to go into the matter further, figures from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics show that the institutional holdings of farm debt 'by insurance companies, trust loans on mortgages, government agencies, railways and1 other organizations for 1945 were reduced1 to $263 million, whereas in 1938 the figure had stood at $418 million. Surely that indicates that the position of our farm people in respect of the reduction of debt is favourable. If we can anticipate the continuation of prosperity of our farming communities it is only reasonable to expect the lending institutions in this country to give farmers risk capital at a decent rate of interest. I would, therefore, ask the government to give real consideration to bringing the rate of interest dlown to two and a half or three per cent, more in line with the risk involved.
When we find the government putting a prop under private enterprise, as it is doing in this bill to the extent of ten per cent, and when we have the government's own statement that no losses have been incurred1-in other words, when we have prosperity the farmer pays his debts-it is only reasonable to ask the government to give serious consideration to reducing the rate of interest, and not leaving it so that provision is made for a maximum of five per cent, and a lower rate only if the bank sees fit.
While I am on my feet, I would ask the government to give serious consideration to the suggestion put forward by the hon. members for Wood Mountain and Swift Current to the effect that, in respect of crop failure, the farmer, after setting out his loss, should have a crop security, so that in the event of his losing his crop no interest would be payable in that year.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: If the legislation is of any value, why bring it up every three years? The fact is that when the farmer wants an extension of capital it is generally at a time when credit is easy, when money is cheap and he can generally get a loan from the bank. There has been plenty of money available under this legislation for the past three years when things have been fairly good, relatively speaking, for the farmer. The next three years may be years in which our farmers may not want extra capital, but a period may come when there are crop failures and they will want loans. That will be the time when they will need money out of this fund, but they may not be able to get it. This legislation is something like the chap who lends you an umbrella when the weather is fine but who takes it back from you when it begins to rain.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

speechtext:
The act is to encourage the provision of intermediate term and short-term credit. I do not think a $200 loan should be extended for ten years. The regulations which I have cited provide for a maximum term of eighteen months for a loan of $200, and up to ten years for a loan of $3,000. With refer-

ence to the crop failure section, I might say that a bank may, with the borrower's approval, revise an agreement in any way. speechtext:
There has been considerable discussion this evening as to why only $31,000,000 of this $250,000,000 has been used. I think the answer is that we are in an inflationary period and have been almost ever since this act has been in force. I know many farmers who want to repair and build, but if you look at the second to the last report of the Bank of Canada you will see that the building index is at 202. Farmers are frightened of going into debt for many of the things they actually need.
Farm implements were mentioned, and I think all hon. members know that the supply does not begin to take care of the demand. The fact is that farmers fear going into debt to buy things at prices which are rising daily. Electrical appliances were mentioned, but I would remind the committee that, with one stroke of the pen when parliament was not sitting, the cost of those things was increased 25 per cent. It is these and other reasons why greater advantage has not been taken of this legislation.
When the act was brought into being in 1944 we argued that the interest rate should be around three and half per cent. I should like to know upon what basis the present rate was arrived at. The banks charge different rates of interest in the different provinces, depending upon local conditions.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Then the hon. member would say that these higher costs are due to the orderly decontrol?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
I am not saying anything about that. I do not think it will be disputed 
that the figures I have given from government's experts are accurate. As I say, that ia the prevailing situation, and I am sorry to say that it is getting worse instead of better. That is why more use is not being made of this measure. It was stated when it was brought down that it was for the transitional period following the war; that was the reason given at the time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: If a situation should develop such as has been suggested where the demand for loans is greater than the capital available, what will be the governing principle? Will the loans be made where the need is greatest or where the credit is of the best? So far as we are concerned, they should be made where the need is greatest.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: It is up to the manager of the bank. Of course the banks are not run exactly as charitable institutions.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Do you leave discretionary powers to the banks to divide up the loans?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: It is purely discretionary with the banks.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: The hon. member for Melfort asked whether there had been consultation between the department and the banks as to the interest rate in view of these impending amendments, and the reply of the junior parliamentary assistant was that he was not sure whether such consultation had taken place, but no representations, he said, had been made to the banks with regard to the interest rate. I want to make sure whether that is correct, that no representations were made by the department to the banks with a view to having the interest rate lowered.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: I said I did not know of any representations having been made.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: That is an important point, because the information given us earlier was that of the $31,000,000 lent none had been lost in the three years of the operation of the act. One would have thought, therefore, that in the interest of the farmers the government would have sought to have the interest rate reduced. The banks are apparently doing a very safe business under this act. The minister is here now, and perhaps he could tell us definitely whether any representations were made by the government to the banks with a view to having the interest rate lowered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Not so far as I know.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Souris has given us his reason why he thinks more loans have not been made under the act. The high cost of farm imple-

Farm Improvement Loans
ments and other equipment would be a deterring factor in the farmers taking advantage of the act. But I do not agree with the hon. member that this should be a short-term measure.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: I did not suggest that it should be. I said that was the reason given by the government on introducing the bill in 1944.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: There should be a source of credit available to farmers at a low rate of interest so that they can develop their farms efficiently. Out west you can see farm after farm abandoned because during the 1930's the farmers had to pay a tremendous rate of interest to the banks on loans and mortgages on their farms, and hundreds of farmers lost their farms in consequence. As the hon. member for Swift Current said this evening, agriculture is the backbone of this country and, until we get a measure through which will provide credit to our farmers at a reasonable rate of interest, we have no alternative but to support this measure even though it is inadequate to the needs.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: I want to make it clear that I was not suggesting that this should be a short-term measure. I realize just as well as the hon. member for Assiniboia that there is a great need for credit among the farmers, especially of western Canada, and has been for years.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
Paragraph (a) states the purposes for which a loan will be made, and paragraph (b) says:
(b) for any purpose other than that specified in paragraph (a).
Is there any limitation whatsoever on the purposes for which a loan may be made? Or is it wide open for any purpose whatsoever?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: The purposes are specific. It may be to buy agricultural implements or livestock, for alterations and improvements to a farm, for fencing, draining, ditching, construction, repairs and alterations to farm buildings, for the improvement and development of a farm, and general improvements.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: That does not include paying off a debt?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

repayment thereof is longer than five years" intended to qualify paragraph (a) as well as (b)?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: What is the procedure normally followed in making application for a loan under the act? I suppose that a farmer needing a loan goes to the bank and speaks to the manager. Does the manager himself decide on the application without the matter going any farther and there being no appeal from his decision? In other words, is it left entirely in the hands of the bank manager?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: When a borrower wants to get a loan he goes to the bank manager and fills out a form, which is later turned in to the department; and the applicant, when the loan is granted, files a document showing the goods he has bought with the proceeds. At the end of the month the bank makes a report to the department stating that such-and-such a loan has been made.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: That covers the case of a loan that is made. But if the bank manager turns down the request for a loan, the department hears no more about it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Then the department would have no information and no way of compiling information as to the number of applicants for loans who had been turned down ?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: There is no way of checking on loans which have been refused.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext: Will primary producers other than farmers be eligible for these loans?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
I know that this bill is called the Farm Improvement Loans Act. In cases of this kind the general view should be taken that all primary producers should be included. Apparently this bill is for the benefit only of the farmers of Canada.
I should like to be told why other primary producers are not eligible. I will speak of the fishermen. They must have boats and equipment to work with. They must have homes in which to live. Why this discrimination? Why is one primary producer selected to take advantage of these loans and other primary producers not included?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT OF 1944 EXTENDING ITS OPERATION FOR THREE YEARS
speechtext:
If no answer is to be given to the last question I should like to ask a question on section 2. It states that in case the amount of the loan is more than $2,000

the bank can take a mortgage or hypothec upon the farm. Then with regard to foreclosure this might easily happen. The farmer has a loan of $2,000, but the next year he has a crop failure. Is it entirely within the discretion of the bank as to whether or not foreclosure would be entered into? Does the government exercise any discretion or protection in the way of advising the bank as to when it shall or shall not foreclose? In many cases, if the farmer is allowed to carry on for a year or two, even though he cannot make his payment in one particular year, in a couple of years he may be able to make the payments and in that way save his home. In that event he would be able to pay both the government and the bank and save his home. I was wondering whether there was some provision in the act which would carry him over a year or two when, through no fault of his own, he has no income at all.

speechtext:
The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Golding in the chair.
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Excise Tax Act and to provide:
1.	That on and after November 18, 1947, there shall be imposed, levied and collected an excise tax of twenty-five per cent (25%) on the following goods imported into or manufactured or produced in Canada: (a) The following electrical appliances: waffle irons; roasters;
fMr. Gastleden.]
kettles; chafing dishes; juice extractors; coffee makers; toasters of all kinds; portable humidifiers; curling irons or tongs; hair dryers; permanent waving machines and spacers or clamps; rods and heaters therefor; razors and shavers; garbage disposal units; (b) The following electrical appliances when adapted to household use; food or drink mixers; food choppers and grinders; irons and ironers; vacuum cleaners and attachments therefor; floor waxers and polishers; (c) Electric or gas refrigerators or freezing equipment, and coils, condensing or compressor units, cabinets, boxes, evaporators and expansion valves therefor; all the foregoing when adapted to household or apartment use or when for use in places of entertainment, amusement or recreation, including rinks, auditoria, halls and clubs; (d) Firearms except for military or police purposes; (e) Outboard motors; (f) Motorcycles. and all other two or three-wheeled motor-driven vehicles including motors for attachment to bicycles but not including vehicles specially designed for carrying goods or for use by invalids; (g) Projectors for slides, films or pictures designed for industrial or professional photographers' use; (h) Toilet articles of all kinds (including combs, mirrors and brushes other than tooth brushes or shaving brushes the duty paid value or the Canadian manufacturer's selling price of which combs, mirrors and brushes is more than twenty-five cents each) and which items do not already come within any other item in schedule one of the said act.
2.	That on and after November 18, 1947, the rate of excise tax on automobiles adapted or adaptable for passenger use with seating capacity for not more than ten persons each, imported into or manufactured or produced in Canada be increased from ten per cent to the following rates, namely, on automobiles valued at $1,200 or less, 25 per cent; over $1,200 but not more than $2,000, 25 per cent on $1,200 plus 50 per cent on the amount in excess of $1,200; over $2,000. 25 per cent on $1,200 plus 50 per cent on $800 plus 75 per cent on the amount in excess of $2,000.
3.	That on and after November 18, 1947, the rate of excise tax on phonographs, record playing devices, radio broadcast receiving sets and tubes therefor, be increased from ten per cent to twenty-five per cent;
4.	That	on	and	after	November	18,	1947,
the rate of excise tax on cameras, photographic films and plates, projectors for slides, films or pictures, except those designed exclusively for industrial or professional photographers' use, be increased from ten per cent to twenty-five per cent;
5.	That	on	and	after	November	18,	1947,
electricity and gas used in dwellings be exempt from consumption or sales tax; and
6.	That	on	and	after	November	18,	1947,the excise	tax	of one cent per pound	on	sugar,
grape sugar, glucose, sugar syrup, corn syrup, etc., be repealed.

Mr. Chairman, last night the minister gave us what was a drastic revision of the original articles covered by the resolution, and I think I have one or two general questions which

Excise Tax Act Amendment
the minister might perhaps answer now, and which will lead me to other questions. Can the minister give us in some detail a breakdown of the savings in United1 States exchange which were expected to be made? The bill is designed to do two things, to collect taxes and to save United1 States dollars. Can the minister give us, in whatever form is convenient to him, figures which were estimated when the schedules were first prepared, and the changes which will result from the eliminations which have been made?
Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT i(Minister of Finance): No estimates were made as to what the savings in United States exchange might be as a result of the curtailment of consumption in Canada of those articles as a result of the imposition of the tax. Therefore, since no estimate was made, nor do I think it would have been possible to make any accurate estimate, I can give the committee no idea as to what it might amount to.
The minister says that no estimate was made of the saving of exchange. Was an estimate made, of the taxation likely to be collected?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; it was felt that it was extremely difficult to do even that, and I could not give the committee any estimate as to the amount of taxes which would likely be realized from the imposition of this particular tax. There are so many uncertain factors. Perhaps it would be a bit easier to estimate in connection with automobiles than with any other thing; but there again it is hard to say how much the imposition of this tax would, in fact, cause prospective purchasers of automobiles to defer the purchase. Therefore my officials found that it was really impossible to make anything like an accurate estimate of the probable tax realization from the imposition of the proposed tax.

To turn to another aspect of it, I take it that it must be possible for the minister to give us in some detail the reasons for the drastic changes which have been made. They have just been referred to. I should like to hear the minister say something as to the reasons, because the changes have been drastic in1 the extreme.
While I am on my feet, I should like to ask another question. It has been represented to me that actually the falling off which was expected in United States purchases has not taken place. For instance, in electric tableware and that kind of thing, can the minister give figures showing us whether or not the expectations have been realized?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I cannot give any figures. It is probably a little early yet in any event for there to have been any real results which could be shown. A good many of those who were affected by the taxes have made representations to us that orders have been cancelled and that their volume will be substantially reduced. I must say that when I received those representations I had to point out to them, regretfully as it might be, that was one of the purposes which the proposed tax was intended to accomplish. But I have not yet any figures, and I think it would be pretty difficult to give them at this stage, as to what the actual effect of the imposition of the tax would be. There are so many other factors that might influence the purchase of these particular goods that one perhaps could never put one's finger exactly on what the effect of this tax might be.
As to the other point, the reasons for the drastic changes that have been made, as a matter of fact the changes have not been nearly so drastic as might appear. The first change made was the removal of electric stoves from the list of electrical appliances on which it was proposed that the tax should be imposed. The principal reason for that was this. It was represented to me, and I am satisfied that it was the case, that in a great many sections of Canada there was really no alternative form of cooking stove which could be made readily available. One outstanding example occurred in a certain section of the citj' of Winnipeg, and that was true elsewhere. And, since a cooking stove is an essential part of household equipment, it was felt that, much as we would like to reduce, for the time being, the manufacture and purchase of electrical stoves, it would not be desirable to impose a tax on that particular article.
Then there was the case of sporting goods. There it was shown, after discussion with the industry, that in that particular line-tennis balls and that sort of thing-a large export market, relatively, had been built up, a market which would virtually be lost if this tax was imposed1 on these products. In view of the United States customs regulation, which requires a tax of this kind to be included for the purpose of fixing customs duty rates, that would affect these exports, and we found on analysis, on balance, that there would be more United States dollars lost by imposing this tax and restricting domestic consumption, at the same time cutting off exports.
The other example was in connection with certain cases where it was found that the products included were manufactured almost entirely by small industries located in different parts of Canada. Among other things, that
Excise Tax Act Amendment

applied to such items as pleasure boats, which were made by small builders in Nova Scotia and around the great lakes section of Ontario. There it was represented, and we were satisfied that the representations were sound, that the effect of imposing this tax would impose a great hardship on these small builders.
The same thing applied to the piano industry. There are seven or eight manufacturers of pianos in Canada and the import content is negligible. The materials are nearly all produced in Canada. The financial position of the piano manufacturers, while adequate, was not too strong. By that, I mean that the imposition of the tax, it was quite clear, would virtually eliminate for the time being their *prospective sales and would again in these cases cause great hardship.
We came to the conclusion that on balance, weighing all the factors, taking them all into consideration, there would be no substantial saving of United States dollars either directly or indirectly and that on that sort of thing the tax should not be imposed.
There was one other general class. We decided to exclude from the operation of the tax electrical appliances and that sort of thing which were used in the processing of food and so on. That could be more properly handled under schedule III, and the tax would be imposed only where the articles -were going into consumer use for household purposes.
There were other examples. In the general category of toilet articles, it was represented that on the cheaper hair brushes, combs and mirrors and small things the imposition of the 25 per cent tax created an impossible price situation. Again, the import content was negligible, and therefore these were eliminated from the list.
Speaking broadly, over the last couple of months I have received a great many delegations, and a great many individual representations have been made both to myself and to the officers of my department. All have been carefully considered, and where it was
felt that we could appropriately remove articles from the list which was proposed, without seriously affecting the purpose which we had in view, we decided to do so.
That is as detailed a statement as I can give. Every one of these cases has been carefully considered by myself personally after all the facts have been gone into by the officers of the department. I am familiar with and could give to the committee the reasons for each individual change; but, broadly speaking, these were the principles that guided us in making the changes.
Mr. M.ACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario): Do I gather from the minister that the endeavour has been to remove those articles where there was a comparatively small United States content?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is one factor. The other factor has been where the continued imposition of the tax would cause exceptional hardship to the producer involved, beyond what we felt was commensurate with the benefit which we wanted to produce. The third factor, which is really related to the second, was where there were two or three or a small number of relatively small producers who would be seriously affected by a substantial drop in or a complete elimination of their production.
